we identified a novel pathway for the oxidation of methylidyene on Rh{111}.
a novel mechanism for CO2 formation from methylidyne on rhodium is identified and that the microkinetic model based on this mechanism describes the experimental data very well.
the direct oxidation of methylidyene to a surface aldehyde-type species followed by its decomposition is the main reaction route for the oxidation of methylidyine to CO and CO2.

the catalytic formation of syngas from CH.
the adsorption of methylidyne, CH, on Rh{111}.
the oxidation of CH on the Rh{111} surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
methylidyne on a Rh{111} surface is not only a precursor for syngas but also for CO2, depending on the reaction conditions.
our DFT study has shown the existence of a previously unreported reaction route for the oxidation of CH on Rh{111}.
the oxidation of methylidyney to CO2 on Rh{111) is a two-step reaction, with a surface aldehyde as an important intermediate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
methylidyne on the surface of Rh{111} can be oxidized by two pathways: a direct reaction with molecular oxygen and the reaction with surface adsorbed oxygen.
the catalytic oxidation reaction of CH to CO2 and H2O can occur on a Rh{111} surface via the novel pathway, which is a surface aldehyde-type species.
the oxidation of CH on Rh{111}-based catalysts proceeds via a new reaction pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the formation of surface aldehydes is a possible and important pathway for the oxidation of CH on rhodium, which is not only important for the catalytic conversion of methane to syngas but also for the understanding of the catalytic formation of CO and H2 from CH.
the oxidation of methylidyney on rhodium can occur through a novel pathway, in which the methylidyne reacts with O2 to form a surface aldehyde-type species, which is then further oxidized.

the oxidation of methylidyene on Rh{111}: (1) proceeds via the novel pathway of direct oxidation to a surface aldehyde species; (2) is the main reaction mechanism for the conversion of CH; (3) can explain the formation of CO, CO2 and CH3OH from methylidyne; and (4) is a promising route for the catalytic formation of syngas.
